candidateRows: God provides the best and most probable explanation of the universe's most general physical and conscious features.
This states the principal theistic thesis and identifies the four broad classes of evidence on which the ensuing cumulative case depends.
At the beginning of his presentation, Swinburne defines God and identifies the universe, simple laws, human bodies, and consciousness as his explanatory evidence.
Evidence supports a hypothesis when the hypothesis predicts it, its negation predicts it less well, and the hypothesis is simple.
These three criteria supply the inferential framework by which Swinburne evaluates theism and its alternatives throughout the discussion.
After listing the phenomena to be explained, Swinburne introduces predictive fit, comparative likelihood, and simplicity as the governing explanatory criteria.
A perfectly powerful and good God has reason to create embodied conscious agents capable of freely choosing good or evil.
It supplies the positive likelihood claim that theism gives reason to expect the embodied, conscious, morally responsible beings requiring explanation.
Swinburne argues that the cited cosmic conditions enable human existence and that a good God would value creating agents with meaningful moral freedom.
Without divine creation, uniform simple laws and laws capable of producing human bodies would be extraordinary coincidences.
The move supplies the comparative-likelihood component of the case by claiming that naturalism gives no reason to expect uniformity or life-permitting laws.
Having argued that God has reason to create humans, Swinburne contrasts this with an uncreated universe and stresses uniformity and life-permitting fine-tuning.
The God hypothesis is simple because it postulates one being whose essential omnipotence amounts to having no limit on power.
Divine simplicity is required to satisfy Swinburne's third explanatory criterion and complete his claim that theism is a probable explanation.
Swinburne closes his initial case by treating unlimited power as simpler than an arbitrarily bounded capacity and linking creation to valuable human agency.
The theistic argument is rationally applicable to everyone because it uses the same explanatory criteria employed in scientific inference.
This establishes the intended epistemic ambition of the case and defends its method by connecting its likelihood and simplicity criteria to scientific practice.
Oppy's question whether the argument supports only permissibility or rationally obligates everyone.
In response to Oppy's question about ambition, Swinburne invokes Newtonian theory choice to argue that theism is assessed by universally rational scientific criteria.
Opposing assessments can be challenged at identifiable errors, while fine-tuning objections about parameterization are answered by privileging the simplest formulation.
The response defends objective comparative assessment and preserves the fine-tuning inference against the objection that reparameterization changes apparent probability ranges.
Oppy's challenge that Mackie applied similar standards to the same evidence yet reached the opposite conclusion.
Swinburne says Mackie's reasoning can be disputed point by point, then argues that the simplest scientific formulation determines which constant and range matter to fine-tuning.
Fallibility and judgment make it unwarranted to dismiss philosophical opponents as irrational merely because they reject one's argument.
The move presses a methodological consequence for the claimed universal rational force of Swinburne's case and challenges his treatment of informed disagreement.
Swinburne's account of Mackie's error, fallibility, and the rational status of disagreement over the argument.
Oppy interprets Swinburne as acknowledging possible mistakes and judgment calls, then argues that branding all dissent irrational would amount to philosophical hubris.
Theism should be evaluated through Bayesian odds against an equally detailed naturalistic rival rather than considered as an isolated hypothesis.
This reframes the central dispute as an explicit comparison between elaborated theism and naturalism across likelihood, prior probability, simplicity, and total evidence.
Swinburne's Bayesian presentation of theism through hypothesis-centered explanatory criteria.
After closing the disagreement exchange, Oppy proposes an odds form of Bayesian comparison in which detailed theism and naturalism compete on the total evidence.
Swinburne's second criterion already makes his reasoning comparative, while polytheistic and limited-deity rivals lose on simplicity.
The response directly defends the comparative adequacy of Swinburne's method and begins ruling out salient theistic alternatives on his key simplicity criterion.
Oppy's proposal to use Bayesian odds to compare equally elaborated theism and naturalism on all evidence.
Swinburne answers that a rival explaining the data equally well would defeat his second criterion, then argues that many gods or bounded gods are less simple.
A simple naturalistic initial singularity with an inherent disposition to evolve could explain all subsequent data without adding God and could therefore be simpler than theism.
The model directly challenges the claim that naturalism must posit innumerable unexplained similar particles and supplies a competing simplicity comparison.
Swinburne's claim that naturalism leaves uniform laws, initial conditions, and innumerable similar physical entities inadequately explained.
Oppy proposes a single simple initial state with powers yielding particles and later complexity, while acknowledging that actual pre-inflationary cosmology remains unsettled.

Oppy's physical initial state would require highly specific powers to produce embodied conscious beings, whereas theism explains those life-producing powers through divine reasons grounded in goodness.
This is the principal theistic response to the proposed naturalistic rival, relocating complexity from the number of initial objects to their finely specified causal powers.
Oppy's proposed naturalistic singularity whose simple initial disposition allegedly explains later particles, bodies, and all observed data.
Swinburne grants that the rival begins with one object but argues that its physical powers must contain extensive detail directed toward producing laws, bodies, and persons.

If actuality determines modality and possibilities should not be multiplied beyond those required by the actual world's indeterminism, then the initial state and laws are necessary and their necessity explains why they obtain.
The proposal directly supplies a naturalistic answer to the demand for explanations of the laws and initial state, thereby contesting a central claimed advantage of theism.
Swinburne's contention that a naturalistic starting state must have unexplained, highly specific powers and conditions built into it.
Oppy first notes that theism may likewise encode much in its initial posit, then develops an actualist account on which laws and initial conditions had to be as they are.
God is not a gratuitous extra entity because one omnipotent and perfectly good being provides a simple reason for a universe arranged to produce finite moral agents.
The move answers the naturalistic simplicity challenge by claiming that divine nature unifies both the production of humans and the value-directed structure needed to produce them.
Oppy's Bayesian claim that adding God makes theism more complicated while providing no improvement in explaining the observed data.
Swinburne argues that recognizing goodness motivates an omnipotent being, who lacks temptations toward evil, so the production of valuable finite agents follows from divine nature.

Treating the universe as arranged for human beings is gratuitously anthropocentric because the observed world contains vastly more beetles and stars and might equally be described as arranged for them.
The objection attacks the evidential premise that humanity is the salient result requiring a value-based divine explanation rather than one outcome among many abundant phenomena.
Swinburne's claim that the universe's production of human beings is explained by their distinctive goodness and God's motivation to create them.
Oppy invokes the abundance of nonhuman life and astronomical objects to dispute the assumption that human beings identify what the universe is fundamentally set up to produce.

The theistic explanation need not claim that humans are the universe's only good; finite agents have the distinctive good of choosing between good and evil, which gives God a special reason to create them.
The reply refines the proposed divine reason for embodied conscious agents and addresses the charge that the argument arbitrarily ignores other valuable features of creation.
Oppy's objection that selecting humans as the purpose of the universe is gratuitous given the much greater abundance of beetles and stars.
Swinburne accepts the goodness of stars, plants, and animals but maintains that morally limited agents instantiate a value unavailable to a necessarily good omnipotent deity.
Mind-brain identity theory offers a particularly simple account of consciousness because mental states and processes are physical states and processes of organisms.
The proposal supplies a naturalistic account of consciousness against the contention that consciousness resists physical explanation and therefore supports theism.
Swinburne's claim that consciousness does not fit established physical science and has not been shown to follow from organized matter.
Oppy notes Swinburne's earlier dismissal of identity theory, defines the theory, and argues that its ontological economy may let it explain the same evidence more simply.

Mental properties cannot be identical with physical properties because physical properties are publicly accessible whereas subjects have privileged, noncontingent access to their own thoughts and experiences.
This is the substantive argument for rejecting the principal naturalistic explanation of consciousness, preserving consciousness as evidence needing a different explanatory account.
Oppy's defense of mind-brain identity theory as a simple explanation identifying organisms' mental processes with their physical processes.
Swinburne contrasts publicly observable mass, size, and charge with a subject's immediate access to thought and feeling and others' apparatus-dependent access to them.

Even if physicalism about mind were false, naturalism could allow minds to arise from physically complex organisms through a natural process, adding only limited complexity rather than decisively favoring theism.
The answer separates naturalism from strict physicalism and denies that failure of identity theory would automatically transfer the explanatory advantage for consciousness to theism.
The audience's proposed implication that falsity of a physicalist or materialist theory of mind would increase the evidential case for theism.
Oppy concedes that a nonphysicalist naturalism may be somewhat more complicated but argues that emergent minds through a metaphysically natural process remain a live possibility.

Theism predicts the general existence of embodied, conscious, finitely free moral agents rather than every human detail, because bodies localize agents and permit them to affect one another against their wills.

The distinction between predicting a broad valuable kind and predicting its contingent implementation directly addresses whether theism's many possible creations undermine its likelihood for observed beings.
The audience challenge that God could realize conscious moral goods in innumerable ways, so theism may poorly predict the particular world observed.

Swinburne concedes many possible bodily forms and powers while maintaining that limited conscious agents need some public localization enabling reciprocal constraint and morally significant interaction.
Embodiment need not involve matter, but it must provide a determinate location through which agents can affect and be affected by others.
The clarification supports the theistic explanation of embodied agents by specifying the functional feature that any acceptable embodiment must possess.
Oppy's suggestion that divine signaling among minds could permit interpersonal interaction without bodily beings.
Oppy proposes a form of theistic idealism; Swinburne accepts nonmaterial implementations while retaining publicly accessible location as functionally necessary.
Objective comparative priors are available because scientific theory choice relies on simplicity measured by entities, properties, and mathematical relations.
The move supplies the epistemic foundation for assigning theism a comparative prior and therefore underwrites the debate's probabilistic comparison.
The audience objection that unspecified or subjective priors undermine the proposed Bayesian comparison of theism and naturalism.
Swinburne argues that science already uses objective simplicity criteria and that ordinal comparisons of prior probability suffice without exact numerical assignments.
Bayesian comparison may sometimes proceed without numerical priors when one hypothesis has both the higher prior and better likelihood across every evidential partition.
The move qualifies the preceding account of priors and proposes a nonnumeric framework for comparing the total evidential performance of rival hypotheses.
Swinburne's claim that objective simplicity judgments permit comparative prior probabilities even when precise numerical values are unavailable.
Oppy notes disputes between subjective and objective Bayesianism, then outlines sufficient conditions for qualitative theory comparison without assigning probabilities.
The relevant comparison requires theism to be much simpler than its rivals, while cosmological inquiry legitimately depends heavily on priors because little new evidence is expected.
This move strengthens the prior-probability defense by specifying the magnitude of the simplicity advantage and explaining why priors bear unusual weight in cosmology.
Oppy's proposal that qualitative Bayesian dominance can establish comparative support without assigning exact numerical prior probabilities.
Swinburne accepts comparative reasoning but requires a large simplicity differential, then argues that theory choice often must proceed by simplicity when further evidence is unavailable.
Metaphysical possibility is ultimately analyzable through logical possibility and the intelligible conceivability of alternative universes.
The account states Swinburne's modal framework, which bears on the space of possible universes used in comparing theistic and naturalistic explanations.
The question invoking Oppy's branching account of modality and asking Swinburne whether that account affects the broader argument.
Swinburne says the modal disagreement may not alter the debate's conclusion, while grounding possible worlds in conceivability and logical possibility.
Metaphysical modality concerns what exists and must not be explained by doxastic possibility or measures of rational ignorance.
The distinction rejects an epistemic basis for metaphysical possibility and directly challenges the modal framework used to characterize explanatory alternatives.
Swinburne's proposal that metaphysical possibility can ultimately be analyzed through conceivability and logical possibility.
Oppy separates metaphysical facts from what a reasonable person could believe, arguing that ignorance has no metaphysical consequences.
God is not necessary in the fashionable essence-based or logically necessary sense, but the unexplained ultimate cause is ontologically necessary as the final brute fact.
The move clarifies the modal status of theism's fundamental posit and places God and a brute universe under the same ultimate-cause conception of necessity.
The audience request that Swinburne explain and defend whether God is necessary and, if so, in what precise modal sense.
Swinburne denies that God is logically or essence-based metaphysically necessary, while calling whichever ultimate unexplained reality exists ontologically necessary.
Swinburne's ontological necessity closely resembles Oppy's metaphysical necessity, leaving less substantive disagreement between their modal views than their terminology suggests.
The observation narrows the purported modal dispute and prevents terminological differences from carrying unsupported weight in the comparative assessment.
Swinburne's distinction between logical necessity and the ontological necessity possessed by the ultimate unexplained cause.
Oppy interprets Swinburne's ontological necessity as substantially equivalent to his own metaphysical necessity while preserving its distinction from logical necessity.
Adding God can improve a theory's overall simplicity when one new kind of entity explains many otherwise separate facts, because simplicity is constrained by explanatory fit.
The move directly answers the central comparative objection that naturalism is automatically simpler because theism adds God to the natural world.
The objection that naturalism is ontologically simpler because theism retains the natural world while adding a divine entity and attributes.
Swinburne treats simplicity as one criterion within explanatory theory choice and argues that science routinely posits unobservable kinds when they unify otherwise disconnected phenomena.
